Twenty-seven years ago Frederick Banholzer, a resident of St. Paul for twenty-six years, took out his first naturalization papers, at Freeport, Ill., which he subsequently lost. For a dozen years Mr. Banholzer has been trying by letter to get a transcript of the issuance from the Freeport officials, but without success. Finally he gave the matter in charge of Col. Keifer, clerk of the district court, who yesterday received the proper official certificate, upon which he promptly made out and delivered to Mr. Banholzer his second papers, who can now, after being a resident of St. Paul for more than a quarter of a century, consider himself a full-fledged American citizen.

About as abject a looking creature as even a reporter is often called upon to meet in his daily rounds for police happenings, appeared at the municipal court yesterday afternoon, in the person of the fire bug Alonzo Garner, arrested for setting fire to several buildings near the Post Siding, Sunday night. He was ragged to the verge of nakedness, unkempt, whisky soaked, and bloody, and his appearances indicated a most desperate spree. A witness named Bender testified that the prisoner had stated that he was going to burn up the town. Several witnesses testified to having seen him in the neighborhood of the fires just before the alarm, and to the arrest, after which he was almost lynched by the populace. Defendant stated that he had the tremens, and didn't know what he was doing. He was held to the grand jury.

Last evening Officer Shields arrested a man named Donahue for raising a disturbance on Rice street.

The only applications under the new law for permission to carry concealed weapons were made by a clergyman and a journalist.

Most of the buildings that were destroyed by fire on Eighth street, between Cedar and Minnesota streets, about three weeks ago, have been rebuilt in an enlarged form, and are nearly ready for business. The smoke stack of the box factory was being raised and put in position yesterday.

Edward Nacey was before the court yesterday for getting drunk and beating his helpless little children. He is an old timer and his misfortune and brutality is all owing to whisky. He was required to give bonds in the sum of $150, and not having the savors he was committed.

He bore the illustrious name of John Adams and he was before hizzonor yesterday for frescoing the bugle of a man named Loveland. It was shown that the latter had threatened to shoot defendant and he was fined only $5. Not haying the dust he went to quay for five days.

A long time ago when the birds were singing in the morning and the hawthorn and the myrtle were in bloom, George Rierson met and loved a bonnie damsel named Miss McFeegan. A cloud came over their young dream in the form of a relentless papa and big brother, who swore that they would have none of Rierson's in theirs, if the court knew itself, and she thought she did. By and by the McFeegan's gave a party and Rierson was not invited. This was gall and wormwood and he made up his mind to take in the party anyway. He went, and on being refused admission he knocked in the door. The big brother tackled him with a chair and there was a regular picnic. Rierson was arrested and yesterday he was fined $10 and put under bonds to keep the peace.

A Young Bride Becomes Homesick.

New York, Dec. 5.—About two years ago the daughter of Amos Stillman of Brooklyn eloped with W. S. Guild. Miss Stillman was only about 16, while Guild was 70. After the private marriage ceremony they slipped away to Europe, without the knowledge of their relatives and friends. Things were not what the young bride thought they should be, and in four days she became homesick, and prevailed upon Guild to return. When they reached the wharf in New York he hired a coach and sent her home, while he got upon another steamer and set sail for California. For one year he remitted his young bride $18 per week, and then the remittances stopped. Now she sues him for a limited divorce on the ground of abandonment. It is understood that he claims that she abandoned him. On Saturday a motion was made by her counsel for a counsel fee and alimony. It was opposed by counsel for defendant, who said his client was in California, and would have to send affidavits to him. The case was postponed.

Omaha. Neb., Nov. 5.—All Omaha was startled this morning by the announcement in the morning papers that Watson B. Smith, Clerk of the United States Court, had been found murdered at about 2 o'clock this morning at his office door in the third story of the United States Court-House. Col. Smith not coming home last night at the usual hour, his mother became anxious concerning him, and called on Dr. Moore, a near neighbor, to go and look for him down-town. The Doctor telephoned to druggist Kuhn about 2 o'clock to go to Col. Smith's office and see if he was there, as he had been complaining of being sick. Kuhn did so, and found Col. Smith lying dead upon the floor in the hall, in a pool of blood, with a bullet-hole in his head.

THE ALARM WAS GIVEN, and investigation was begun. A revolver of a large calibre was found sticking in his left pantaloons-leg, near the foot, with the butt-end exposed. His key was still in his door, which he was about to shut up on departing. The door was partly open. Two letters which he had written, directed, and stamped were on the floor at his feet, as they had fallen from his hand. It was apparent that he intended to mail them down-stairs in the post-office as he should leave the building. His hat was on the back of his head, full of blood. He had turned out the gas in his office, and the murderer probably turned out the gas in the hall, and laid in wait for him, and, as he was about to close his door, put a revolver to his head and fired, striking above the left temple, the ball.

GOING CLEAR THROUGH THE HEAD and landing on the floor. The revolver that was found did not belong to Col. Smith, which explodes all theory of suicide. Everything shows that the deceased had no idea of the kind, but that he was preparing to go home. His own two revolvers were found at his home. At the Coroner's inquest today several threatening letters were produced. Col. Smith was a prominent temperance man, and had taken an active part to enforce the Sloeumb Liquor law, compelling saloons to pay $1,000 license. He also caused the saloons to close on Sunday. For some time past a bitter feeling has existed toward him on the part of some liquor men on this account. Letters containing threats came from that source, and are villainous productions. The Coroner's jury returned a verdict of murder.

EXCITEMENT AT LINCOLN.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LINCOLN, Neb., Nov. 5.—The news of the shooting at Omaha of Watson B. Smith, Clerk of the United States District Court, was brought into the District Court in this city this morning, and it caused a profound sensation. The Hon. T. Marquette addressed the court, and said that telegrams received from Omaha announced that Watson B. Smith had been murdered at the door of his office at Omaha. He suggested that there be a meeting of the bar of the United States Court this evening, and that his Honor preside. Mr. Marquette further remarked that Mr. Smith, in his office, had been a friend and helper of the attorneys who practiced in the United States Courts. For the past five months he had been actively engaged and endeavoring to enforce the laws in this city as well as in Omaha. Lawyers knew the necessity of enforcing the law, and the good which follows such enforcement. He hoped, therefore, every member of the bar would be present to honor the memory of one who had sacrificed his life in support of the laws of his country. In compliance with the suggestion of Mr. Marquette, a full representation of the bar of Lincoln is now in public meeting at the United States Court-House, and speeches are being made in relation to the sad affair. The people of Lincoln, and especially the legal fraternity, are horrified over the assassination. Every particular in relation to the same is eagerly caught up and discussed by our people, and the greatest sympathy is felt for the immediate friends and relatives of the deceased. Col. Smith was well known in this city, and bore the reputation of being an excellent citizen and a bold and outspoken friend of law and order.

Details of the Crime and Execution of Bob Williams-Another Negro Narrowly Escapes the Same Fate.
Williamston Correspondence Charleston News and Courier, 4th.
About 7 o'clock this morning two of our best citizens drove into town and lodged in the guardhouse a negro whom they had arrested in Greenville county some time during last night. It was soon ascertained that the negro had, a few days ago, outraged a little nine-year-old child, the niece of one of the gentlemen who had him in charge. The little orphan girl was living with a Mr. Clark between Greenville and Macloy's factory, who, yesterday, as soon as he discovered what had been done, brought her to her uncle in a fearfully injured condition. That gentleman, who, though a preacher, is noted for his nerve and pluck, procured the aid of his nearest neighbor, and going very quietly to the home and bed of the fiend who committed the awful deed, tied him hard and fast. His first question was, "Are you going to kill me?" While coming to Williamston he begged his captors to stop and shoot him. He said his former master had often told him he would be hanged some day; that his time had come; he was guilty, and wanted to be shot.

At eight o'clock, about one hundred men assembled at the depot to do justice to the prisoner and justice to the poor little outraged orphan child. This crowd was made up of young, old and middle aged men, all anxious to learn the particulars and pursue whatever course the facts of the case might demand. After some consultation it was determined to take the criminal back into Greenville county and there mete out to him such punishment as in their judgment his conduct deserved. Though he had boldly contessed his guilt time after time, two of the crowd were appointed to take him to the little girl and have him identified. She did identify him, and while the demon stood in the presence of his innocent victim, he said, "Yes, that's the little girl." His doom was segled. He was marched across the bridge over the Saluda river, at Pelzer, just two miles from this place, and there on the hill opposite that beautiful and growing town, was hanged until he was "dead, dead, dead."

That is the closing chapter in the life of Bob Williams—a demon too flendish to be buried in the soil that contains the ashes of human beings. Our streets have been very quiet ever since the very orderly crowd marched the culprit away to the last scene of his life. I am informed this evening, however, that after things had quieted down this morning, and the laborers at Pelzer had returned to their work, a negro, whose name I did not ascertain, remarked that if the dead man had been anything to him he would not have suffered him to be killed for that offense. He was instantly seized by some of the same crowd that had hanged the other negro, and with a rope around his neck was being hurried off to the spot that was made memorable by the incidents of the hour before, when President Smythe and Mr. Caughfin interfered, and after begging hard for him, had him released, with the promise that he would never more be seen in Anderson county. David R. Locke, ("Petroleum V. Nasby") has returned from Europe. His letters to the Toledo, O., Blade were exceedingly interesting and instructive. Mr. Locke before visiting Ireland and while in England was a bitter denunciator of the Irish, charging them with being lazy and thriftless. Their complaints and the agitation of the Land question he regarded as unfounded. After visiting Ireland his opinions on this subject underwent a complete change, and he is now one of the ablest champions the Irish have in this country. His descriptions of Irish suffering, of which he was an eye witness, are vivid and powerful. He characterizes the treatment of Ireland by the English government as brutal in the extreme and a disgrace to civilization.

LYNCHING AT BAY ST. LOUIS.
Our Bay St. Louis correspondent has furnished us with an account of the lynching of the colored man Charles Stewart, at that place, last Monday night for the murder of his wife. Lynch law is a dangerous precedent, even where proof positive can be established, but much more so where the evidence is circumstantial, as we learn is the case in this instance. The man who was hung bore a very bad character, and it is asserted had killed a man sometime previously, but these facts do not justify the hanging of him without a fair and impartial trial, which he could have obtained before the circuit court at its next sitting.

If mob law is allowed to usurp the regular legal course of courts in a community there will be no security for law-abiding and peaceable citizens, for there would be no telling when any innocent man may be jerked up and swung into eternity; society will be demoralized, and good people will be forced to leave and never return. We learn that the best citizens of the Bay condemn this recent act of the lynchers, and will take steps to have the guilty ones indicted and punished, and will do all in their power to put down all such acts of violence. Certainly something ought to be done to put a stop to such illegal and revolutionary acts, and the sooner the people understand such proceedings will not be tolerated the better it will be for the community and society.

Charles Stewart, the negro who was jailed here on suspicion of killing his wife, was brought before Justice Sylvester on Monday and put under a bond of $1000 to appear at the circuit court for trial; failing to give such bond he was recommitted to prison, and placed under the protection of the officers of the law. The county prison is a sacred place, where the innocent and the guilty are under the protection of the laws, and when circumstances make it necessary it should be properly guarded.

During the investigation of this case before the Justice, it was shown that he was a man of intemperate habits and violent temper; that he had often whipped his wife, and perhaps had, on one occasion, threatened to kill her. It was evident that the witnesses were, in some instances, what the law books term "swift witnesses," and had made up their minds as to his guilt. There is a strong presumption that he really was guilty, but there was no positive proof, no eye witness of the bloody deed. Every one knows how deceptive circumstances are. God alone knows who committed the foul murder.

All day, 15th., a crowd of colored people was gathered in and around the courthouse, men and women, vowing vengeance. They took up a collection, bought a rope, and kept it on exhibition, declaring their intention to hang the prisoner. The only peace officer to be seen was Louis Paoli, constable. The day closed amidst this excitement. No guard was placed about the prison, and about midnight the mob hewed down the strong gates and doors of the jail, took the prisoner out and hung him. At a late hour on Tuesday his body still swings, a ghastly spectacle, to testify to the supremacy of MOB LAW at Bay St. Louis.

The same thing may occur again and again, unless sternly repressed by the next grand jury. Every man concerned, their aiders and abettors, is responsible for this man's life, to the laws of his country. Public opinion, here and elsewhere, demands a thorough investigation. Next time we shall hear of a white man being taken out of jail before trial, and hung by a negro or a white mob. Open the door for those violations of law and there is no longer security here for life and property.

A few weeks since a young white man shot a negro, as he claims, to save his own life. The friends of the wounded man were greatly excited, and openly proclaimed their intention, in case of his death, to lynch the assailant!

How much such a state of thing will conduct to the prosperity of Bay St. Louis its citizens can determine for themselves.

MANY towns and villages in Western Prussia have recently suffered much from incendiary fires. The fact that the inhabitants are Jews leads to the conclusion that the incendiaries are Jew-haters. Anti-Jewish disturbances have again broken out in West Prussia and Pomerania.

THE Nebraska Supreme Court has rendered a decision that the high-license liquor law is constitutional in every particular. It compels saloon-keepers to pay $1,000 license, give bonds in the sum of $5,000, etc., in cities of over 10,000 people, and in cities of under 10,000 the license is $500.

THE large woolen-mills in Iowa belonging to the Amana Society, valued at $75,000, have been destroyed by fire.

THE Atlantic Flouring Mills at St. Louis were entirely destroyed by fire, caused by a lightning stroke, on the night of the 12th. The flames burst forth so quickly following the stroke, and spread so rapidly, that the men at work on the upper floors, a dozen or so in number, were completely hemmed in and were compelled to jump from the windows. All were severely burned and otherwise injured, and two of the unfortunates died during the night. It was feared that several perished in the flames. The mills were the largest in St. Louis, having a capacity of 1,200 barrels a day. They were owned by the Atlantic Milling Company, George Bain, President, and the total value of buildings, machinery and stock was estimated at about $250,000. Insurance from $75,000 to $100,000. The mills have been three times destroyed by fire. Considerable surrounding property was burned, the most important being the Future City Oil Works, valued at $25,000.

An express train on the Grand Trunk Railway was thrown from the track near Prescott, Ont., on the 13th, caused by the locomotive striking a cow. The locomotive and tender and express-car were overturned and completely demolished, and four passenger coaches were derailed. The engineer stuck to his locomotive and met a most horrible death. The fireman was pitched off by the concussion and badly injured. Two express messengers and a baggagemaster were buried beneath the debris of their car and rescued in an almost dying condition. Nine passengers were injured, six of them seriously.

THOMAS A. CRANDALL, a prominent Colorado stock dealer, fell from the top of a cattle train at St. Joseph, Mo., on the 13th, and was run over and killed.

E. M. MARKS, of Rome, Ga., and C. M. Creswell, of Mebanesville, N. C., students at Eastman's College, Poughkeepsie, N. Y., while boating on the Hudson River were run down by a steamer and both were drowned.

An emigrant train ran into a washout near Las Vegas, N. M., on the night of the 12th, killing engineer Townsend and fireman Patton.

By the sudden falling of an old building in one of the most frequented quarters of Vienna, on the 13th, twenty persons were killed and thirty injured.

CHARLES BOYNTON, a mill hand at Portland, Me., attempted to kill his wife, who had left him and gone to her mother's at Bar Mills. He fired at her with a revolver but missed, and she saved her life by jumping from a second story window. His wife's sister, Mrs. Waterhouse, then entered the room, when he fired two shots at her, one of which entered her breast inflicting a probably fatal wound. Boynton then shot himself through the pit of the stomach, expiring instantly.

MAXIMO JAREZ, the Minister from Nicaragua to the United States, died of apoplexy at Washington.

The drouth in Switzerland has continued for nearly two months. The grass is burned, and in the mountain pastures beasts are perishing from heat.

A band of cowboys recently attacked a caravan from Sonora on the way to Arizona, killed four of the party, and carried off $5,000 and the pack animals. The civil authorities in Arizona seem powerless, and the Mexicans hold the Americans responsible for the outrages.

Three negroes lay down on the railroad track near Tuscumbia, Ala., and fell asleep. A freight train came along and killed two of them and seriously injured the third.

SHOT DEAD.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Oct. 10.—Intelligence reached this city today of a terrible tragedy last Saturday at a sawmill near Grand Lake, Ark., a small town on the Mississippi River. William Brooks, proprietor of the sawmill, was beating on employe when a fellow workman named Willian Yountz interfered. Brooks, exasperated, turned upon Yountz, when the latter drew a revolver and fired, the ball striking Brooks in the head and killing him instantly. Yountz was arrested, and after a preliminary examination was discharged.

St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 16.—The body of an unknown man was found yesterday hanging to a tree in thick woods four miles from Grain Valley Station, on the Chicago & Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City. Evansville, Ind., Oct. 16.—A colored man named Green was found dead in the suburbs of Henderson this morning, with his head split open with a cooper's adze. A man was arrested on suspicion and lodged in jail. The adze, covered with blood and hair, was found two squares from the body. It is supposed he was murdered for his money.

CHICAGO, October 16th.—Startling figures are given, showing a great and steady increase in scymatic disease, which, according to the State Board of Health, is due to the unclearly condition of the streets, and in a less degree to a large influx of the low classes of immigrants. Week before last there were 36 deaths from typhoid fever, and the number this week is still greater. In January there were 18 deaths from small-pox, in May 46, in August 116, in September 108, and so far in October 79. The entire mortality from small-pox in 1870 was 18. Unless there is a decided reform in the street cleaning methods, even greater mortality is probable.

William H. Vanderbilt on Wednesay went from New York to Albany in his special car in three hours and twent-five minutes, or at the rate of about eighty-three miles an hour.

The Providence Journal says that the bodies of five persons have been taken from the Providence River inside of 18 months whose death has not been satisfactorily accounted for.

The Troy Times says that Mrs. Sarah M. Gould has paid a judgment of $500 and costs, in all about $1,000, obtained by a Lansingburg boy named Jocko, who was bitten by a dog owned by Mrs. Gould.
gran-valley-station-gran-valley-station-.A14:
Miscellaneous Items.
St. Louis tobacco market (Oct. 22); Dark lugs, common to good, $5.00 to $6.25; bright smoking, common to good, $6.00 to $7.00; dark red leaf, $6.50 to $8.50; half-bright wrappers, common to medium, $10 to $18.

The St. Louis Republican, of a recent date, says: Mr. P. Van Frank, civil engineer of the St. Louis, Iron Mountain & Southern Railway, has returned from making the reconnoissance for a branch road through several important counties of Missouri. The projected line starts from Iron-dale in Iron County, and runs through Iron, Washington and Dent Counties to the southern line of Texas County, where it strikes the Kansas City, Springfield & Memphis Railroad. The length of the line will be about 110 miles, and will tap a fertile and richly-timbered country, giving St. Louis another valuable railroad tributary.

Curtis Goddard, an aged and blind wood-sawyer of St. Joseph, has received official notice of the allowance of a pension of $22 per month, with $9,700 in arrears. While in the army he contracted a disease which has not only wrecked him physically, but his eyes soon went out. For ten years he has made a very meager living by sawing wood.

It is understood that Allen Parmer, the brother-in-law of the James boys, has dismissed his suit for $40,000 against Superintendent Treat, of the United States Express Company, and ex-Marshal Liggett. Parmer sued for damages for false imprisonment. He was arrested in Texas for participation in the Glendale affair, but was never indicted. It is now stated that Parmer has been arrested for complicity in the Winston affair.

Reuben Grigsby, youngest son of Mr. A. W. Grigsby, an old and respected citizen and farmer of Mississippi County, committed suicide a few days ago by shooting himself in the center of the forehead with a rifle, which killed him instantly. It is said he had been very despondent during the week about what he termed a failure of his corn crop.

The St. Louis freight blockade still continues.

A very mysterious hanging is reported from Grain Valley, in the southwestern part of Jackson County. A farmer going through a dense woods was horrified to find the dead body of a man with a rope around his neck lying on the ground under a tree, while suspended from a limb above was another piece of the same rope. The farmer immediately gave the alarm, but all efforts at identifying the deceased proved a failure. One theory is that he was a detective and met his fate at the hands of the train robbers; another is that he was a horse-thief who met with summary punishment from the farmers of the vicinity. The third, and most reasonable proposition is, that the man committed suicide.

The twenty-seventh annual session of the Grand Lodge of I. O. G. T. of the State of Missouri convened at St. Louis on the 18th. Wm. F. Switzler, of Columbia, Grand Worthy Chief Templar, presided. The report of the Grand Worthy Chief Templar showed that the organization now numbers about 550 lodges, with an aggregate membership of 29,000 persons, and holds the position of banner Grand Lodge of the world.

A Monroe County man has trichinosis.

The Grand Jury at Independence have indicted John Bugler, John Land and Creed Chapman for participation in the Blue Cet train robbery on Sept. 7 last, and their trial has been fixed for the February term. Sam Chapman, captured at the same time, is held on an indictment for carrying concealed weapons, and he has made a statement in regard to the train robbery which will be used as testimony against the others. The Court of Appeals has refused to interfere in behalf of Kotovsky and Kring, the St. Louis murderers, now under sentence of death. In many orchards in Phelps County deach trees are in full bloom.

james-truss-desoto-1881-10-01.A1:
MISSISSIPPI MATTERS.
Moss Point has the measles.

DeKalb is to have a new courthouse.

N. I. Smith died near Senatobia last week.

Mrs. Ike S. Harvey, of Holmes county, is dead.

The Pioneer says Walthall needs a shoe-maker.

William Hester has been appointed Postmaster at Terry.

Major J. L. Wofford, of Corinth, has declared for Lowry.

The Jackson Clarion records the death of Rev. T. W. Hines.

Mrs. Fannie Hudspeth died in Water Valley on Monday last.

The Baptist State Convention meets in Meridian on the 20th instant.

Dr. Morgan Adams, of Sardis, a dentist of ability, has removed to Jackson.

A half interest in the Homestead and Observer, at Meridian, is offered for sale.

Colonel J. J. Williams has again assumed the editorial chair of the Grenada New South.

The Democracy of Calhoun county have nominated R. N. Provine for the Legislature.

Hon. J. S. Montgomery, a prominent Republican of Adams county, has declared for Lowry.

Mr. M. A. Dees has sold his interest in the Democrat-Star to Messrs. M. B. Richmond and George W. Wilkes.

The State printing under Radical rule cost $100,000 annually; under Democratic rule it costs $25,000 annually.

William Allgood, an old and esteemed citizen, was found dead in his bed near Brookhaven, a few days since.

Hon. E. Henderson, of Harrison county, is the Democratic nominee for State Senator from the Seacoast District.

The Jackson Clarion is authority for the statement that Major Barksdale is not a candidate for the United States Senate.

Captain E. O. Sykes has been nominated for the Legislature in Monroe county, and this by acclamation, which means election.

Charles A. Hamilton, Esq., has purchased an interest in the Wesson Herald and taken control as editor and business manager of that paper.

The people of Scott county did a good thing for themselves when they re-nominated Judge Lyle for the Legislature. So says the Carthagenian.

Hon. C. V. Gwin, of the Lexington bar, will soon take the stump for the Lowry
Carthaginian.
Hon C. V. Gwin, of the Lexington bar,
will soon take the stump for the Lowry

ticket, and continue in the field till the close of the canvass. He is a fine speaker and ranks among the best lawyers in the State.

H. O. Eaton was shot and killed on Friday night last at Bunker Hill, Smith county, by Dan Hathorn. As soon as Hathorn shot Eaton, Dick Yawn shot Hathorn and killed him. Both Eaton and Hathorn died instantly.

The State tax in 1875, under Radical rule, was $9 25 on the thousand. The State tax under Democratic rule in 1881, is $3 on the thousand. The State tax under same rule in 1882 and 1883, may not exceed $2 on the thousand.

Five miles from Crystal Springs there was a boiler explosion last week, in which one white man and a colored man were killed, parts of the body of the colored man being carried 200 yards. Two others were badly wounded.

When the Republicans ruled the State, Kimball, Raymond & Co. charged fifty dollars for a six quire docket. J. L. Power does the work for twelve dollars—a difference in favor of Democratic rule of thirty-eight dollars on one book.

The tax levy in Hinds county in 1874, under Republican rule, was $224,731 27, and in addition, during a period of five years, a debt of $150,000 was created. The present tax levy of the county is $73,869 71, including the additional railroad tax.

Mississippi has provided handsomely for the education of her sons, both white and colored, in the liberal support annually given the University at Oxford, Alcorn University, the A. and M. College at Starkville, and the Normal school at Tugaloo.

Of the 760,000 square miles of timber lands in this country, the South owns 460,000, or nearly two-thirds. They will be mines of wealth in a few years. Mississippi, and especially the pine-wood counties, will come in for a large share of this wealth.

We learn from the Copiahian that Dan Coor's steam-mill, located in Copiah county, blew up on the 18th ultimo, killing two and severely wounding and scalding six other men. Dan Coor, the proprietor, was a young man of great energy and business capacity.

John Hicks, who some weeks ago eloped with the wife of Mr. G. W. Eggerton, who lives about twelve miles east of Shubuta, has been arrested and ledged in the jail at Quitman. They went to Monroe, Louisiana, where they were married and honey-mooned awhile.

Joe Thomas, the murderer, who was brought to Jackson from Arkansas, was taken to Vicksburg Saturday by Sheriff Joor, of Sharkey county. He was placed in the Vicksburg jail for safe keeping, there being a disposition on the part of citizens of Rolling Fork to lynch him.

The Kosciusko Star states that the gin-house of W. H. Stamfield, of Holmes county, was accidently set on fire last week by a lamp in the hands of an employee named Johnson. Johnson was in the lint-room, and before he could get out was so badly burned that he is not expected to live. The gin-house, with all its contents, was entirely consumed.

Last Saturday night an inoffensive and peaceable colored man named James Truss was killed at Desoto, by being stabbed in the neck. He only lived a few minutes after being stabbed. It is said that the following named persons were concerned in the matter: Burt McRee, Young Nealy, Cook Johnson and Cooper Morris, white, and Royal Evans, colored.

Governor Stone has appointed ten delegates to the Mississippi River Convention, to meet in St. Louis on the 26th of this month, as follows: H. P. Reed, Friars Point; James L. Alcorn, Jonestown; Green Clay, Bolivar Landing; General S. W. Ferguson, Greenville; Captain S. H. Parisot, Lee Richardson, George M. Klein, of Vicksburg, and John A. Dicks and J. W. Lambert, of Natchez.

The Jackson Clarion has come out very decidedly in favor of separating the judiciary from the executive department, whereupon the Free Press says: "It is about three-thirds right, but a little late in presenting its arguments. Several years ago would have worked as well, and would have been much better for the Democratic party. However, better late than never, and it is hoped the Clarion will have sufficient help."

Hon. Charles B. Howry has returned to his home in Oxford from the mountains of East Tennessee, but we regret to say with his health but slightly improved. The Eagle says: "He is one of the rising men of our State, a forebite and eloquent speaker, a true Democrat, and worthy of any honors in the gift of the people. He has entered actively upon the canvass and will strike telling blows for the Democratic cause."

jas-browning-st-joseph-1881-07-04.A1: At St Joseph on the 4th a crowd of roughs, headed by a cripple named Bruce, attempted to pur all colored people off the exposition grounds. Jas. Browning, colored, had his skull fractured; a white man, who interfered to protect him, had his jaw broken, and sustained other injuries; a colored lad named Fowler was beaten into insensibility; an old colored man named Harris was struck with a chair, cut with a knife, and injured so badly that he died and other colored men were badly injured. A little girl was run down by the city marshal and had her leg broken. The military was summoned and with additional police force the riot was quelled. There is terrible excitement over the affair.

Call Out the Troops.
Call Out the Troops.
San Antonio Express.
The people down about Larodo.
The people down about Laredo do not seem to like the idea of a colored inspector being appointed to keep an eye on them. A mulatto by the name of Samuel R. Hurst, from New Orleans, has recently assumed the duties of inspector, or river guard, and the people are rebellious. A gentleman just up from Laredo reports that Hurst was shot at three or four times the other night, and barely escaped being killed.
laredo-laredo-1881-09.A3:
CRIME.
In an affray at Lick Run, O., Richard Williamson shot James and Scott Tipton, the former fatally.

ALDERIAN PITTS, a wealthy farmer near Murfreesboro, Tenn., was assassinated in his melon-patch, evidently because he had commenced a divorce suit.

A negro river guard at Laredo, Texas, has several times been fired upon, it is believed by Mexicans, on account of his color.

The embezzlement of ex-Secretary Stuart, of the Brooklyn board of education, is now shown to be $107,500, and he has been rearrested.

ELLA St. CLAIRE, formerly a variety actress, in Mobile, married a negro, who was indicted for miscegenation, whereupon she sprang into the river and ended her career.

OTWAY B. ZANTZINGER, a young merchant of Baltimore, a nephew of Mrs. Admiral Farragut, has been arrested and sent to St. Louis for obtaining under false pretenses $7,000 worth of flour.

GEN. MORTON, the swindler, has reached Richmond, and the police are anxious to prevent a lynching. Miss Turpen, the victim of one of his bigamous marriages, lives in strict seclusion in that city with her widowed mother.

In the Jennie Cramer murder case, at New Haven, Henry C. Allen, a printer, has identified James Malley, Jr., as the person whom he saw riding with the murdered girl on the night of Aug. 5 which is considered a point of the greatest importance.

POLICE CAPTAIN HATHAWAY, of Chicago, went to Milwaukee in search of Nolan, who murdered a dock-laborer in a saloon on Michigan avenue. The man he sought resembled Nolan, but had lost no front teeth, which was positive proof of being on the wrong track.

GEN. MORTON, the bigamist and swindler, was taken from the train on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., and quietly placed in jail. His appearance has undergone a wonderful change in a few weeks, but the detectives say it is simulated. A showman offers $600 for the privilege of exhibiting him for one night.

A CLERGYMAN of Dayton, O., writes to the authorities of Richmond, Va., that he united in marriage an estimable lady and Morton, the bigamist, the latter giving the name of Lieutenant-Governor Miller, of Minnesota. This is the fifteenth matrimonial victim of the prisoner.

THOMAS H. LOWERRE, a compositor employed on the Chicago Tribune, was shot dead by his landlord, James B. Duncan, a photographer doing business on State street. The deed originated in charges of criminal intimacy between Lowerre and Mrs. Duncan. The killing was preceded by a furious fight, in which Duncan's shoulder-blade was broken.

Two men known to be robbers entered the train at Comstock's N. Y., and information was telegraphed to Albany and Saratoga officers. In an effort to capture them near Mechanicsville one of the thieves shot Deputy Sheriff Port, of Saratoga, in the neck. The fire was promptly returned, the robber being hit in the forehead. The accomplice undertook to run away, and was shot in the neck by a farmer.

linden-linden-1881-07-10.A1:
NEWS FROM OUR NEIGHBORS. TEXAS. Last Thursday Dr. H. J. Avinger, who resides on the East Line railroad, not far from Jefferson died of wounds received some days before at the hands of a negro, Hicks Ross, who disembowel him with a knife. The murderer was arrested and confined in Linden jail. FLORIDA. In the Gulf off Pensacola, at the red snapper banks, some days since, the water was so hot in the well of a fishing smack that about half a cargo of snappers died. The vessel returned to the banks, caught more fish and preserved them alive by some of the crew getting down into the well and keeping them constantly in motion. The fish seemed to become stupid and drowsy, evidently overcome by the heat, but their method of keeping them on the move enabled the fishermen to reach port with a profitable catch. They report like experience in years gone by, but not on so extensive a scale. ARKANSAS.
ARKANSAS.

During the past year two hundred houses have been built at Little Rock.

Near Ozark, last week, Fred Choate, a horse-thief, committed suicide to keep from being arrested.

A panther which has been preying on stock between Kensett and Searcy, has again made its appearance.

An oil-mill and cotton compress is to be erected at Fort Smith under the direction of Zeb Ward and E. Urquhart.

At Wiley's Grove, Van Buren county, a few days since a little daughter of M. Hatchett was tossed on the horns of a vicious cow and severely injured.

ALABAMA.

At Bridgeport last Friday an elopement was prevented by the indignant father and brother of the young lady, who intercepted the young couple at the depot, and presenting pistols at them, the bride was taken home by the father and the young man was ordered to leave.

On Thursday last, at Randolph, a negro entered the bedroom of Mrs. Hudgins, wife of the bridge foreman of the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia railroad, and attempted to outrage her person. She escaped from the room to the yard, where the negro caught her, and a desperate struggle ensued. Her cries brought assistance, and the villain fled and escaped. She received several blows on the head, and her throat and arms were severely bruised.

MISSISSIPPI.

The machinery for the Yocone cotton

MISSISSIPPI.

The machinery for the Yocona cotton mills has been received at Water Valley.

The storm of last week blew down nearly all the corn between Artesia and Columbus.

Anthony Fallelove, a negro who is under sentence of death, has again escaped from the Vaiden jail.

Near Fulton, several days since, Monroe Roberts committed suicide by shooting himself with a pistol. Cause, insanity.

At Water Valley last Sunday night a lamp broke in the Presbyterian church, setting the building on fire. The congregation extinguished the flames.

Last Wednesday night the residence of W. B. Saunders, four miles south of Grenada, was destroyed by fire. Cause, incendiarism. Nothing was saved from the building.

At Grenada, a few days since, J. W. Holland secured a judgment for $1000 damages against George W. Beard, Circuit Court Clerk, because the latter had issued a marriage license to Holland's daughter, she being under the age of eighteen. The case was appealed.

TENNESSEE.

Fine crops are reported from Haywood county.

At Chattanooga, last Friday, a man named Jones, from Ringgold, got into a row with Peyton Gray, a colored barber, and stabbed

Gray in the head twice with a knife and escaped.

Cashman, Bailey and Williams, the safecrobbers, are on trial at Brownsville.

A new Roman Catholic church is to be erected at Knoxville at a cost of $25,000.

Last week, in Wayne county, a yoke of oxen was killed while lttched to a tree during a thunderstorm.

Last week, near Lynnville, the residence of Joe P. Boyd was burned to the ground. Nothing was saved. No insurance.

At Chattanooga a general dog-killing progresses favorably. Dogs of both high and low degree unmuzzled become victims.

A gray eagle, seven feet ten inches from tip to tip, was recently killed near Rogersville. Its talons were covered with sheep's wool.

At Columbia last Saturday William Porter was shot dead in a saloon by Hugh and Sam Cook. Six or eight shots were fired. The Cooks were arrested.

Last week, near Brownsville, Gus Bolling, colored, was killed by the sides of a well caving in upon him. His cries for help were heard for several hours.

The Press and Times says the Courthouse at Rogersville has for years been a gambling hell, made so by disreputable parties who play cards therein at night.

Neal's State Gazette is out again, but in small size. It will soon be republished with new type and from new presses. Colonel Tom Neal is not the man to back down from a fire.

Near Columbia, at the Old Wellgrove, a debate is progressing between J. B. Martin, of the Church of Christ, and H. Bellap, o the Church of Latter-Day Saints, on the subject of Mormonism and divine inspiration as to the Mormon Bible and King James's version of the Scriptures.

Last week, at Knoxville, a dead white child was found in a vault on Methodist Hill. The jury of inquest discovered it to be the child of Harriet Kellar, a white girl. It was born alive, but no evidence of violence was found on its person. The girl was arrested on a charge of infanticide.

A recent shipment of 150,000 feet of Dyer county timber has been made direct to France. The logs were "squared up" in the woods, and the ends well oiled to keep the sun from cracking them. They were then rafted out of the Forked Deer to New Orleans, from which place ships took them to France.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A2:
TEXAS TOPICS.
Waco had a splendid and most enjoyable celebration of the Fourth.

Genuine cotton worms have been found in some fields in Rusk county.

Mrs Jane Glow died suddenly Sunday morning in Sherman at the age of thirty-two years.

Mr. W. T. Lane and Miss Mollie E. Smith were married in Smith county last week.

James R. Seely, Esq., a prominent young lawyer of Mexia, died of black jaundice on the 4th.

Sue Allen, a colored woman at Waco, accidentally shot her hand off with a pistol on the Fourth.

The celebration of the Fourth at San Antonio is represented as having been a very tame affair.

There were fourteen deaths in Houston last week, one from drowning and five were children.

There is a great deal of sickness in Franklin county, but of a mild form being thermic fever generally.

There were seven marriages in Harris county last week and fourteen persons went to that matrimonial borne whence they will never return.

Fifteen thousand persons are said to have been present at the celebration at Denison on the Fourth.

The mortality among the children in Sherman and neighborhood during the past two months is alarming.

The condition of the corn crop in Walker county is deplorable and cotton is suffering because of the long dry spell.

Miss Georgie Johnson was thrown from a buggy at Bastrop Sunday, being painfully bruised and dislocating an ankle.

An excursion train of nine coaches filled with colored people from Houston went to San Antonio on the Fourth for a holiday.

The track of the International railroad is completed sixty miles west of San Antonio, and trains are running to a point fifty-four miles west.

D. P. Morrison has been appointed judge, and John D. Morrison district attorney, of the thirty sixth district. Both are residents of Aisscosa county.

Ed. Moore, one of the supposed Davis state police murderers of Hause and Gadbold at Tyler, eight years ago, was arrested at Jefferson on the 4th.

The corner stone of a new Episcopal church at Bastrop will be laid on August the 11th Bishop Gregg and other divines of that church will be present.

Rev. Dr. Kavanaugh, late of Houston, but now of Kentucky, and seventy-six years of age, married a buxom young widiw at Mt. Sterling, Kentucky, a few days ago.

A new street railroad company has organized at Houston and from the names to be seen among the officers and directors, it is evident an abundance of money is behind the enterprise.

Dysentery of a most malignant type is epidemic in some portions of Rusk county, and prevails to such an extent that there are not well people enough to wait on the sick or bury the dead.

The Lamar county horticultural society gave its third annual exhibition at Paris on the fourth. The display of vegetables was not so large as last year, but there was a vast attendance.

All the milk drinkers at a boarding house in Sherman were made sick by the milk they drank on the Fourth. A physician who was summoned, said the cows had been eating some poisonous weed.

The Good Hope western association of colored Baptists will convene at Marlin on the 14th inst. and remain in session several days. A Sunday school convention will be held at the same time.

The capitol commissioners have adopted the Herald's suggestion, and will invite each county in the state to contribute a representative stone, appropriately inscribed, to be placed in the new capitol.

The advertisement for bids for the erection of the new state house is to be published four times in the New York World, Chicago Times, St. Louis Republican, Dallas Herald, Galveston News, Houston Post, San Antonio Express, Jefferson Democrat and Austin Statesman.

The teachers' normal schools, now going on, are not supported by the state or in any wise under the control of the state authorities. They were inaugurated and supported out of the Peabody fund, and it was as an agent of this fund that Mr. Hollingsworth went north for the teachers.

A telegraph operator at the stone quarry of the Gulf Colorado & Santa Fe railroad near Brenham, was struck on the head by a man named Nicholson, Sunday, and painfully though not necessarily fatally hurt.

A majority of the city council of San Antonio will resign to keep from obeying the mandamus of the federal court at Austin to levy a special tax to pay a subsidy voted years ago, to a proposed railroad from Indianola to that city. In the meantime the case will be carried to the United States supreme court.

A correspondent of the Henderson Times, signing himself Suggs, announces that he discovered a comet in the heavens a few morning's ago, a while before daylight, as he happened to be gazing northward, and he hastens to inform a startled world of the fact. He ought to have that Rochester $200 by all means.

George WLynchwhose house and children in it, was burned near Hoxley some time ago, was convicted of murder in Leadville a few days ago. He always suspected a certain man of burning his house and children and swore he would kill him, and it is supposed this is the man he killed at Leadville.

Dr. H. J. Avinger, wounded by a negro some ten days ago, died on the 30th ultimo.
Dr. H. S. Avinger, wounded by a negro some ten days ago, died on the 30th ultimo. A post mortem examination revealed the fact that two of the intestines had been cut, and gangrene ensuing, death resulted. From accounts of the affair it was an unproycked and most malicious murder, yet the murderer was granted bail in $2,500, which he has been unable to give.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A3:
is parched and almost ruined for want of rain.
Dich Wood, a notorious character in Western Texas, was taken from the sheriff, who had him under arrest, by vigilantes, on the 26th, near Cariso, and shot to death. The vigilance committee, in that part of the State, has been previously unheard of.
On Saturday, the 25th ult., at Avenger Station, on the East Line railroad, Dr. H. J. Avenger engaged in a row with a negro, during which the latter slashed the doctor across the bowels with a razor, inflicting a mortal wound.
A report from Piedras Negras says that several American engineers were killed in the interior of Mexico recently, in consequence of a dispute regarding the right of way, but it is impossible to get any reliable particulars of the affair.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A5:
Marshall.
Marshall, July 12.—The county of Harrison having been added to the third United States collection district, Mr Umbdenstock, the collector will continue to make his headquarters at Marshall.

The Dixon Car Work here are booming. A large force was added last week and more are expected this week. Those employed recently are skilled German workmen, who were brought from St. Louis and will add two hundred to the population of Marshall. The new importation will arrive Friday.

It is rumored, and pretty well confirmed, that the negro who killed Dr. Avenger, at Avenger station, in Cass county, was taken from the jail by a mob on Sunday and hanged. The rumors are confirmed by telegraph dispatches. The Linden jail is one of the strongest in the state and great violence must have been used.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A6:
will hold their annual re-union at Corsicana, on the 3d proximo.

Bellville, on Tuesday, voted in favor of corporation for school purposes, by a majority of twenty eight votes.

Considerable sickness prevails at and around Marquez, in Leon county, and a number of deaths have resulted recently.

San Antonio has two clubs, one an anti-treating club, and the other a club to accept all treats offered but never to reciproscate.

Dr. M. C. McGregor, of Wesley, was shot through the leg, both bones being broken, on Sunday by the accidental discharge of a pistol.

The Tyler branch of the teachers' normal school was opened Tuesday morning. Prof J. R. Horne, of Alleytown, Pennsylvania, in charge.

Two hundred new hands, skilled Germans from St. Louis, have been added to the force of workmen in the Dixon car works at Marshall.

From almost every portion of southern, western and central Texas comes the glad tidings of heavy rains and rejoicings of the farmers.

A son of Mr. Kirkpatrick, living at Lampasas Springs, was thrown from his horse, Tuesday, and so seriously injured that he was not expected to live.

Some of the tooth doctors in the state are beginning to ask for a dental department in the state university. That is getting down to the root of the thing.

Dr. L. S. Rayfield, formerly a physician of Jefferson and then of Austin, died at Atlanta Georgia, on the 7th inst. and was buried at Jefferson on Sunday last.

The corn crop in Colorado county is fair and the cotton very fine. The boll worm has made its appearance in some localities, but Paris green is being freely used.

The case of the state against Reuben, Henry and Williford Laggins for murder, in Waller county, has been set for the 18th inst. at Bellville on change of venue.

The Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad seems to have benefitted Bellville very much, as the place is rapidly improving, with new brick buildings going up on every hand.

A man named Abe McCarty had a preliminary examination at Weatherford, Tuesday, on charge of assault with intent to rape Mrs. Watson and was admitted to bail in the sum of $1000.
A heavy rain and wind storm prevailed at Navasota and that vicinity Sunday, and the residence of Mr. Varnadoe, three miles from Navasota, was blown off its foundation. Nobody was hurt.

Two men in San Antonio claim to have seen an aerolite fall into the river back of their place of business a few nights ago. The spirits commonly used in San Antonio is calculated to make men see aerolites in fact a whole menagerie.

Miss L. M. Crunk, living at Gause, went to visit a neighbor, Mrs. R. S. Cox, Tuesday morning, and when near the house was attacked by a vicious dog belonging to Mrs. Cox. She was badly bitten on the arms and legs and Mrs. Cox in rescuing her was also bitten.

Additional testimony in favor of Wm. Burton, under sentence of death at Weatherford, was mailed to the governor on Tuesday, and it is hoped his sentence will be commuted to imprisonment. A belief in his innocence seems to be gaining ground, as some developments are slowly coming to light to establish that fact.

The Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad opened business at Belton on the 16th of last February, and up to July 1st, a little over four months, the tonnage received at that point was 10 833 042 pounds, and the amount forwarded 3 288 509 pounds. The tonnage shipped consisted of 2 315 bales of cotton and seventy-five car loads of grain with some sundries.

There seems to be little doubt of the lynching of the negro who murdered Dr. H. J. Avinger in Cass county recently. He was confined in the Linden jail, and when Dr. Avinger died of his wound public sentiment was so strong against the perpetrator of the heinous deed that it would not await the slow process of the law, with its delays and uncertainties.

Sheriff Brown, of Lee county, returned to Giddings on Monday with a man named George Keith, charged with the murder of a man named McFall several years ago. A man named Lasion was arrested at the time and trled for the murder, but was acquitted as he was innocent. Subsequent events led to the suspicion of Keith, and after several years he was traced to Sabine parish, Louisiana, where Sheriff Brown arrested him on requisition from the governor.

There is a camp meeting going on at Live Oak, in Hill county. Last Monday evening a young gentleman named Massey went to the meeting in company with two young lady friends and took his seat with them, as seems to be the custom now everywhere unless it is in remote country communities, but in a little while he was waited upon by two men who notified him that he must move his seat over among the men. Dan Emmett, the old-time negro minstrel, is still performing in the West. He is the author of "Way Down South in Dixie," which was first a "walk round" chorus, written in 1859, for Bryant's Minstrels, then at Mechanic's Hall, Broadway. Emmett lately said to a Cincinnati Enquirer reporter: "I wish I was in Dixie' was a Northern circus expression, and not a Southern one, as many have supposed. I had traveled a great many years with circuses in my younger days, and 'the South' was then considered all that portion of the country below Mason and Dixon's line, called for short "Dixie," by showmen. In the early Fall of the year, when a frost would sometimes overtake a south-bound circus still in the North, the boys would think of the genial warmth of the section they were heading for, and many's the time on such an occasion have I heard them say, 'Well, I wish I was in Dixie's land now.' Two years afterward the rebellion broke out, and Emmett's air, which had become popular in the South, was made the representative tune of the rebels. AN ADJOURNED INQUEST.
A murder, which seems the more horrible and atrocious when the deed is contrasted with the youth and innocence of the victims, was discovered in the county Saturday evening. At what time the murder was committed is still a mystery, as is also the manner of the crime, and the name and motive of the murderer. The murder occurred on the farm of Joseph Fisher, a market man, which stands on the Fort Bunker Hill road, about a mile north of Brooks' station, in the county. Here Fisher lived with his wife, and widowed sister-in-law, and the two children of the latter, Lizzie, aged six, and Joe, aged three years. Saturday the older members of the family came into the city to attend to their business, and left the children—as they were accustomed to do—alone in the house. Mr. Fisher returned to his home from the Northern Liberty market about six o'clock Saturday evening, drove his wagon through the grounds to the barn, noticing as he passed near the house the children lying on the ground near to trees.

THE MURDER DISCOVERED.

Having attended to his horse he walked to the house and thought he would wake the children, whom he believed were asleep. When he approached them the sight that met his eyes was horrible. They were beyond waking. Their clothing was stained with blood. The girl's skull was crushed in, and there was a terrible wound on the boy's forehead. Mr. Fisher at once gave the alarm. The police of the second precinct were notified, and an investigation of the murder was begun at once. Mr. Fisher returning to the city, took his wife home, who was at the market and the mother of the children, Mrs. Simon Fisher, who is employed as a domestic in the family of Mr. C. Horner, who keeps an eating house on 9th street, opposite the Center market.

ARRESTS MADE.

The first arrests made by the police were those of Mrs. Christina Taylor, and her daughter, Rose, two colored women, living in a stone house on Fisher's place, just at the gate leading from the main road to Mr. Fisher's house. Mrs. Taylor was arrested because she was seen to leave Fisher's house in the afternoon by the farm hands working near by. Yesterday Thomas Goff, grandson of Mrs. Taylor, was arrested. Coroner Patterson held an inquest yesterday morning, and as little light was thrown upon the murder after all the available witnesses were examined, adjourned it until Wednesday next.

SCENE OF THE TRAGEDY.

Fisher's house, which is a neat little cottage, stands among the trees on a little eminence off from the road. It faces south. The children were found at the northwest corner of the house, about thirty feet away, lying between two trees, a walnut and a cedar. Near them was an axe, which had been left in the morning at the wood pile northeast of the house. Some suppose that this weapon had been used by the murderer, though there were no marks upon it. The face of the little girl was placid and she appeared to have died without a struggle. The boy had one arm over his face, and seemed to have struggled. Ephraim Barnes and two colored men, who work on the place, were hoeing in a field southeast of the house in a hollow about 150 yards away. The house was exactly between them and the spot where the bodies were found. These men saw the old colored woman, Taylor, leave the house about four o'clock, their attention being attracted to her by her efforts to get rid of a dog which pursued her, barking furiously.

The Coroner's Inquest.

Yesterday the inquest was held at the house. The following jury was empaneled: James McNabb, jr., W. H. Harvey, John B. Lord, Elbert G. Benson, Lewis Behrens and Francis Oxraneter.

The first witness was Ephraim Barnes, who works on the place, boarding with the family. He testified that he was at work in the field near by with the colored men; that everything was quiet about the house till three or four o'clock in the afternoon, when the dogs made a racket, and looking up he saw an old colored woman coming away from the house; that one of the colored men told him that it was the old woman who lived at the gate; that Mr. Fisher returned home at six o'clock, and about ten minutes afterwards called, and witness ran to the house where he found the children dead; that the colored woman afterwards returned to the house, and he asked her what she had been to the house for, to which she replied that she came to return a washboard; that she had knocked at the front door about half an hour, and could neither see nor hear anyone; that about seven o'clock he saw her again west of the house, apparently looking about the bushes, he asked her what she wanted and she said: "I thought I heard somebody halloa;" he asked her what she had done with the washboard, and she said she took it into the house and set it down by the table in the back room; that she had got in and come out by the front door; that the washboard was found where she said she put it.

Thomas Ham, colored, one of the men working with Barnes, testified to seeing the old colored woman leaving the house.

Margaret Lynch, a neighbor living at Fort Bunker Hill, testified that Rose Taylor came to her house, apparently much excited, about a quarter after 7 o'clock, Saturday evening, and called her nephew, who worked there, saying that he must come at once.

THE UNCLE'S STORY.

Joseph Fisher, uncle of the two murdered children, testified that they were his brother's children, and had lived with him for two years; that he came home Saturday evening between 5 and 6 o'clock; put the horses in the stable, and as he returned to the house found the children dead; that the old colored woman Taylor had picked peas for him some time; he only knew of her coming to the house to borrow the washboard from his wife; the dog would generally bark at her when she came; there was no trouble with the mother of the children about them; she was willing to have the children at the house, and he and his wife liked to have them.

Dr. Hartigan, who made the autopsy, assisted by Dr. Wolhaufter, testified to having found a transverse wound, lacerated and elliptical shaped, ⅛ of an inch long, above the boy's left eye, and another of the same nature diagonally above and behind the left ear; besides several bruises of the scalp, indicating repeated blows by a blunt weapon. The skull was extensively fractured and crushed in two or three places. The examination of the little girl showed a wound of the scalp above the right ear, another below, and a smaller one three inches above the ear, and there were bruised spots on the same side of the head. The skull was extensively fractured, and the brains were exuding. These wounds, the doctor thought, were made with the same weapon as was used on the boy.

Thomas Goff, colored, grandson of Christina Taylor, testified that he was tending cows for Mr. Lynch on Saturday; that his Aunt Rose came for him while he was at supper, and said she wanted him at home; she said nothing about the children being killed and he did not know about it until that (Sunday) morning; he had not heard his grandmother say anything about the children; she did not seem excited, but her aunt did.

Peter Overton, colored, who lives at Major Goodloe's place, near by, testified that when passing the stone house Saturday evening, he asked the old woman (Christina Taylor) where her daughter was. She jumped up and said: "Go away man I don't want anything to give."

The mystery surrounding the tragedy at the village of Queenstown, reported in the Herald of Sunday last, was solved this afternoon. Christiana Taylor, an old negro woman who was arrested for the murder of the little boy and girl, aged three and six years respectively, on the farm of Joseph Fisher, on the Bunker Hill road, near this city, on Saturday last, confessed to-day that she committed the deed. She has heretofore denied all knowledge of the crime. This afternoon she sent for Captain Vernon, of the police, and Mr. Archibald White and to them made the following confession: "I was going along the path. It was not God Almighty, but it was the devil that put it in my head to kill them. I could not help killing them. I did it, not with the axe nor the washboard, but with a piece of wood, as big as my arm and about eighteen inches long. The children were running about the yard of the house. I struck the one with the long hair first, but I don't know how many times I hit her. I saw the axe in the woodpile after hitting them with the stick. What I killed them for I don't know; the devil got into me so that I could not help doing it. I picked the stick up in the road. I never told any one about it but you and Mr. Arch White. I believe it has worried me some. I have told the truth to you, white people. It is the truth from my heart. I threw the stick away down by the woodpile."

At the conclusion of the confession Christiana was removed to the jail. On the way down she seemed deeply depressed and talked but little. In reply to a question by Police Lieutenant Johnson she said:—"I could not help it. I hit the girl three times, when the boy caught me about my legs and screamed, and I then hit him on the head. I do not know how the Christmas tree came to be by the side of the dead children."

DISAPPEARANCE OF THE WEAPON.

A thorough search was made this afternoon for the stick of wood, but no traces of it could be obtained. It is supposed that if she did use a stick as her weapon it was used the night of the murder in the stove, as a hot fire was kept up in the stove all of Saturday night. It is claimed by some, particularly the colored people, that the woman is insane, and the testimony of Rose Taylor, her daughter, is liberally quoted. Rose in her testimony before the Coroner's jury yesterday said:—"Mother sometimes has giddy spells and behaves strangely. When she came back from Fisher's house Saturday she said, in a very excited manner, 'The Fisher children are dead and we must leave,' and directed me to go at once for my nephew, who works for Mrs. Lynch. Often when she has the spells she threatens to knock us down with a stick of wood." The colored people living in the vicinity of the house of Mr. Fisher have manifested considerable feeling concerning the murder, and have congregated nightly in the neighborhood of the police station where Christiana and Rose were confined. While they were not ready to believe that Christiana committed the deed, yet they were anxious that the perpetrator should be brought to justice. Rose will be detained as a witness to appear before the Grand Jury, which meets September 12. A singular fact in connection with this case is that there is not a living witness to her having committed the crime. When the Coroner's jury yesterday was ready to make up its verdict the testimony, although strongly circumstantial, was of such a character that the verdict had to be worded in the following language:—"The jury are unable to say positively by whose hand the deed was committed, but from the evidence adduced the suspicion points strongly to Christiana Taylor as the guilty party."

The Great Summer Danger.
The burning of a hotel at Beach Haven last Wednesday night will be very apt to make sojoiners at summer resorts nervous, and more afraid of fire than ever. And well may it have that effect. The danger from this source is greater than most persons suspect, unless they have carefully considered the subject and coolly calculated the probabilities of a fire, in the first place, and, secondly, the chances of escape in case one should occur. The fact is, that most of these summer hotels are merely vast tinder boxes, constructed with little reference to the prevention of a conflagration, and provided with few or no means or subduing one should it once get started. The chances are, therefore, at least ninety in a hundred that a fire breaking out in a watering place hotel will result in the total destruction of both building and contents; and we may add that if the inmates escape with their lives they may count themselves fortunate, indeed.

How can the matter be helped? It is hard to say. From the nature of the case, the situation is surrounded with difficulties, the number and character of which make it almost if not entirely impossible to provide complete security. Manifestly the expense of constructing a fire-proof building for a hotel to be occupied only two or three months in the year would be so great, and make the cost of staying in it so high, as to put that provision entirely out of the question. Neither is it possible to provide in all cases a supply of water sufficient to amount to anything in a fight with the flames. There seems to be left, then, nothing but vigilance and caution,—on the part of host and guest alike; and these ought to be exercised always, and in the extremest degree. No person should ever become an inmate of one of these mammoth establish-
uight to be exercised always, and in the extremest degree. No person should ever become an inmate of one of these mammoth establishments for a night—or of any hotel, for that matter,—without first becoming entirely familiar with all its stairways, passages and exits, and deliberately planning a route of escape in case of fire or any alarm of danger. These precautions should then be supplemented on the part of the guest with the greatest possible care in the use of matches, lights and fires. On the other side, the management of a hotel owes it both to itself and to its customers to use every means within reach to prevent the occurrence of a fire, as well as to keep the danger from it within the smallest limit possible. In this direction certainly nothing should be accepted as an effort in good faith which does not include the furnishing of reliable fire extinguishers, and also a plentiful supply of well-filled water-buckets in every hall of the house, together with a vigilant watchman on every floor, whose duty it should be to keep awake and constantly patrol all its passages the whole night through. These precautions ought to be required by law of every hotel situated remote from first class means of subduing a serious fire; but, law or no law, proprietors ought to take them, and the public should make it a point to studiously and firmly decline to patronize any house where they are not afforded.

The murder of the Fisher children is the most shocking crime that has been perpetrated in this vicinity for a long time. It was simply the act of a fiend. There is that in a little child which appeals to every sentiment of humanity. Its very innocence and helplessness inspire within the heart that is not devoid of every human sensibility a feeling of tenderness. It was evident that these two children, scarcely more than babes, had been killed without provocation of any kind. They were incapable of provoking an attack. Now, the mystery as to who perpetrated the act has been cleared up. The old negro woman, Christina Taylor, has confessed the inhuman, the monstrous deed; but the cause or motive for it remains unexplained. She does not pretend to assign any reason for the fendish act, which, it is easy to believe, must have been committed under some sudden and insane impulse. Still, that plea can hardly be successfully urged in her defence. The murderess was sane enough to conceal her guilt as best she could, and the welfare of society requires that she should be made to pay the extreme penalty provided by law for her offence.

The Fisher Murder.—The negro woman, who was charged with the murder of the Fisher children (an account of which was given in the SENTINEL last week) near Brooke's Station, on the Metropolitan Branch R. R., has since made the following confession to Capt. Vernon, of the Washington police, which appeared in the Washington Post of the of the 12th instant:

I was going along the path; it was not God Almighty, but it was the devil that put it into my head to kill them. I could not help killing them. I did not do it with the ax, nor the washboard, but with a piece of wood as big as my arm, and about eighteen inches long. The children were running about the yard of the house. I struck the one with the long hair first; but I don't know how many times I hit her. I saw the ax in the woodpile after hitting them with the stick. What I killed them for I don't know. The devil got into me so that I could not help doing it. I picked the stick up in the road. I never told any one about it but you and Mr. Archie White. I believe it has worried me some. I have told the truth to you white people. It is the truth from my heart. I threw the stick away down by the woodpile.

The circumstances leading up to this confession are worthy of note. Without this statement or the discovery of some more direct evidence, it was the general opinion no case for even the Grand Jury could have been made against the woman. Lieut. Johnson, who has charge of the precinct in which the murder took place, determined to let nothing be left undone to unearth the criminal. The old woman had dropped hints about having something to tell. This Mr. Johnson wished to take every advantage of, but in such a way as not to vitiate the coming confession for use in court. On Wednesday, after the inquest, Christina said to Officer Rhodes, "If I tell, won't it be worse for me?" He replied that it would not.

The circumstances induced the delay in sending her to jail. Lieut. Johnson then decided to hunt up the people with whom the woman had formerly lived. She had mentioned Mr. White's name and he was seen and asked regarding her. Nothing of a dangerous tendency had shown itself in her conduct while with him. He came down, however, yesterday morning at Lieut. Johnson's suggestion to see if she would not talk to him. She at once intimated that if her children were there she would make her statement. Lieut. Johnson started for one of the girls. While he was away Capt. Vernon called to him and Mr. White. She after being cautioned, made her confession. After the statement was made she let fall other additional particulars. When she was beating the girl's head in the baby brother plead for his sister, clinging to her knees and crying. Neither of the children made any loud outcry.

As soon as Lieut. Johnson returned and learned what happened he determined to place the guilty wretch beyond the reach of certain parties whom he knew to be only awaiting her certain identification as the murderess to lynch her. He therefore procured a grocer's wagon, and drove rapidly off to jail. On the way she made the following additional statement:

The devil sent me up there. I tried to fight against him, but I couldn't. I struck the girl first; I struck two or three blows and she fell down. I struck them with a stick, not with the ax. Just as they fell I let them lay. I don't remember seeing the Christmas tree at all. I don't know how it got there.

On Saturday morning when picking vegetables for market the children found some white flowers and told Mrs. Fisher to give them to the Virgin Mary, the youngest adding, "hoping that she will make me a good boy, and keep the niggirs from killing me."

The Alarming Reports
of lawlessness in the Kanawha mining regions, that have been lately telegraphad to the papers, led your correspondent to make a special visit to the scene of action. The facts may be summarized: At Coal Valley about 500 men employed in soft coal mines have been on a strike. They would not work themselves, and did all they could, short of violence, to dissuade others from doing so. The operators brought negroes from Virginia to take their places. The first batch were dissuaded from work by the striking miners. The troops were then called for. The peace was not broken nor was there any sign of trouble beyond the power of the civil authorities to control. The officers themselves admitted this, and I think the people generally regard the calling for troops as premature, and a serious mistake on the part of the Fayette authorities. The demand once made, the Governor could do nothing but comply.

The Question at Issue
between the miners and their employers is one not easily settled. The operators sell their coal to the railroad company, getting ninety-five cents per long ton, or less than three and a half cents per bushel. They pay the miner sixty-two and a half cents per ton; and to the land owner a royalty of fourteen cents per ton, besides ordinary running expenses, making the coal stand in the cars nearly what they get for it, and leaving them as margin nothing but the profits on the goods sold to the miners from the stores. To pay the increase of fifteen cents demanded by the miners is impossible unless the railroad should concede an advance on the price paid the operator. The miner, on the other hand, claims that he cannot live at sixty-two cents per ton. When employed he can make, one day with another, about one dollar and fifty cents per day net. Out of this he must pay six dollars a month house rent, and provide for his family. This he might do if the work were constant, but the railroad will not furnish cars to the operator more than half the time.

So the miner must live a year on the proceeds of six months' work. Lately there was an advance of fifty cents per ton in market, and the miners insist this advance should be divided between the railroad, the operator and the digger. The C. & O. railroad insists, however, upon taking all, on the ground as alleged that heretofore it has been carrying coal at a loss in order to keep the mines running and give the men work.

I think this railroad should be relieved from duty as a philanthropist. A law restricting railroads to their business as common carrier, preventing them from speculating in the industrial products along their line and requiring them to furnish cars for all freight that offers, would seem to be about the proper remedy. It would at any rate simplify matters by eliminating the railroad from the complication, allowing the operator to hunt his own market and make his own contracts, and leave him and his miners free to adopt a sliding scale adjusted with reference to the market price of coal. Such a scale is adopted at Campbell's Creek, where millions of bushels of coal are mined without a word of dispute and without a day's strike.

Policies.

You hear more of politics in this county than anywhere else in this section. In former years the Third district had no other interest save in politics, parties, conventions and candidates.

From every neighborhood the small fry politicians went out to disport themselves in the pool of which Charleston was the center, and the District the circumference. It is not so now.

At college the class in rhetoric used to have as an example of anti-climax the following poetical lines:
“Roll on, thon Connecticut, long hast thou ran,
Bringing shad to South Hadley and freedom to man.”

Still roll the Guyandotte and Kanawha as of old, from the solitude of sang-bearing wildernesses, and the sublime mysteries realms whence come forth vast Democratic majorities, dread, fathomless, inscrutable. But statesmanship now seldom troubles these blue waters with its canoes and keels.

“Shad to South Hadley and freedom to man,” no longer form the sole burden of the country’s business. The talk is of trade and telegraphs; mines and mills; timber and tobacco, and railroads and the restless elements of practical civilization. Here in Mason the idea that office-holding is the chief end of man still has its tenacious hold upon the public mind, but even here I can see something of an abatement of the popular passion. Time was when Mason county could furnish the material for both State tickets and have a surplus left for Congressional purposes.

Now, if she can have Barbee on the Independent ticket for Congress, with Hogg or Schon to oppose him as the Democratic nominee, with the understanding that some other Mason statesman is to succeed Davis in the Senate, and John English can have reserved for him a seat on the Supreme Bench, I think even Mason’s appetite would be sated.
